notes.meaning: Jesus told his followers a story to teach them that they should always pray and never give up. Believers must keep talking with God, especially when facing hard times and waiting for his help. Even if an answer takes a long time, we must not lose heart.

Jesus described a judge in a certain town who had no fear of God and did not care about people. A man in his office was supposed to defend justice, but this judge ignored both God's law and human opinion. He cared only about himself.

A helpless widow repeatedly came to this judge, begging him to protect her from someone mistreating her. Widows in that day had little power and were often cheated out of what was rightfully theirs. She was not asking for revenge, but for the fair protection of the law.

For a long time, the judge refused to do anything to help her. Eventually he thought about his situation and admitted to himself that he did not fear God or care about anyone else. He knew he was selfish and unfair, but he had no desire to change.

The judge finally decided to give the woman justice simply to stop her from bothering him. The words he used compare her constant visits to a boxer beating him black and blue. He helped her only for his own peace of mind, not out of kindness.

The Lord told his listeners to think carefully about what this bad judge said and did. If even an unjust man can be moved by someone who keeps asking, God will do far better. We can be encouraged knowing that God is nothing like this selfish judge.

Jesus taught that God will certainly bring justice to his chosen people who call on him day and night. God loves his children and takes deep interest in their cries. Even when he delays his help to train their patience, he never abandons them.

Jesus assured them that God will act suddenly and bring relief to his people. Then he asked whether the Son of Man will find faith on earth when he arrives. The great danger is not that God will fail, but that people will stop trusting him during long trials.

Jesus told another story directed at people who were sure of their own goodness and looked down on everyone else. People who think they have earned God's favor often despise others. True faith before God is always humble, never proud.

Two very different men went to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee, a member of a strict religious group known for keeping outward rules, and the other was a tax collector. Tax collectors were despised as outcasts who worked for the Roman rulers.

The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed about his own good qualities. He thanked God that he was not like other people, such as thieves, evildoers, and the tax collector nearby. His prayer was really a boast about himself rather than true worship of God.

The Pharisee bragged that he fasted two times a week and gave a tenth of everything he made. God's law required far less fasting than that, so he thought he was doing extra work to earn God's favor. He was completely satisfied with his external religious deeds.

The tax collector stood far away and would not even lift his eyes toward heaven. He beat his chest in deep grief over his sin and begged God to show mercy to him, a sinner. He had no good works to offer and simply trusted in God's undeserved grace.

Jesus declared that the humble tax collector went home justified, while the proud Pharisee was rejected. To be justified means to be accepted by God and declared free from guilt. Anyone who puffs himself up will be humbled, but whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that 'justified' here might not carry Paul's full theological sense of being counted righteous, but simply means the tax collector was pardoned and accepted by God.

notes.meaning: People started bringing even their babies to Jesus so that he could touch and bless them. When the disciples saw this, they scolded the parents for bringing them. The disciples thought infants were too small to understand or benefit from Jesus.

Jesus called the children to himself and commanded the disciples not to get in their way. He explained that the kingdom of God belongs to people who are like little children. No one is too young or weak to receive his love and blessing.

differ.view: Churches in this tradition see this verse as biblical support for baptizing infants, since children of believers share in God's covenant promises.
Baptists teach that Jesus blessed the children without baptizing them, so baptism is reserved for those old enough to profess faith personally.

notes.meaning: Jesus warned that anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will never enter it. Little children cannot buy or earn an inheritance; they simply receive it as a gift. In the same way, we must come to God with empty hands and trust in his grace.

A wealthy Jewish ruler asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. He came with respect and asked the most important question anyone can ask. Yet his question showed he thought heaven was something a person could earn through good works.

Jesus asked the man why he called him good, stating that no one is good except God alone. Jesus was not saying he was sinful, but was challenging the ruler's shallow idea of goodness. If the man truly believed Jesus was good in the highest sense, he should see him as God.

Jesus listed several commandments about loving our neighbors, including honoring parents and not stealing or lying. He pointed to God's law to show the standard required for holiness. He wanted the man to see that no human being can fully keep God's standard.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition teaches that keeping God's commandments is strictly necessary and sufficient for entering into eternal life.

notes.meaning: The ruler claimed that he had kept all of these commandments ever since he was young. He may have obeyed them on the outside, but he did not understand how God's law searches the inner desires of the heart. His answer revealed that he did not yet know his own sinfulness.

Jesus told him that he still lacked one thing: he needed to sell all he owned, give the money to the poor, and follow him. Riches had become an idol in the ruler's heart, competing with God. Jesus showed that true discipleship means putting him above every earthly treasure.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching views giving up all wealth as an evangelical counsel of perfection for those seeking a higher spiritual path, rather than a universal command for all believers.
